## The Product Leader's Edge in 2027: Teams That Talk to Their Own Users


Contributors:


No items found.


Here's some good news to carry into 2027 planning: your team can build almost anything. An idea can become working software in an afternoon, and the cost of trying something new is radically lower than it used to be.


That puts a new kind of advantage within reach: when every team can build fast, the teams that pull ahead are the ones that know what's worth building. The best source of that knowledge is the same as it's always been: the people who use your product, talking directly with the people who build it.


This post covers why that matters more than ever, what it does for your roadmap, your team and your standing as a leader, and how to make it a weekly habit starting this month.


### Knowing what to build is your edge


Andrew Ng, founder of DeepLearning.AI and managing general partner at AI Fund, put it plainly in July 2025:[deciding what to build is the new bottleneck](https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/how-to-get-through-the-product-management-bottleneck) . Determining and prioritizing roadmaps takes judgment, taste, and a deep understanding of your customers. That's the job AI can't do for you, and it's the part great product leaders are best at.


### What we believe at Rally


We spend every day helping product teams get in front of their customers, so we have some strong opinions here:


**Talking to users is a leadership decision.** How often your team hears from customers comes down to what you fund, measure, and celebrate. Nobody else in the company can set that standard for the product org, and when a product leader sets it (and makes it possible), the whole team follows.


**Speed is most valuable when it's pointed at learning.** AI made building fast. The teams we admire use that speed to put ideas in front of customers sooner. A prototype that used to take a month can be in front of customers within days, so the ideas that reach engineering have already earned their spot.


**Real conversations, human decisions.** AI should run the logistics: scheduling, summaries, follow-ups. The conversation with the customer and the decision about what to build stay with people.


### Why your own users are worth more than you think


Dashboards tell you what people did. Your users can tell you why, what they were trying to get done, and what they'd happily pay for. Here's what that's worth to a product org:


**Showing** **you the problem behind the request.** When we hear from customers, it's usually in the form of a feature request. However, in a real conversation, they describe the job they're trying to accomplish behind that request, typically resulting in a better (and smaller) thing to build.


**Raising the value of everything you ship.** Pendo's[2026 product benchmarks](https://www.pendo.io/product-benchmarks/) show that in best-in-class products have a feature adoption rate of only 15.6%. Even the best teams build plenty that customers rarely touch. That's a big opportunity hiding in plain sight: every conversation that steers a feature toward what customers need makes more of your roadmap.


**Keeping** **everyone's assumptions fresh.** Every product team has a few beliefs about customers that nobody has checked in a while. That's normal: we all tend to build for people who think like us. A few conversations a week is the friendliest way to find out where your team's picture of the customer has drifted.


**They're yours alone.** Your competitors can use the same AI tools you do. They can't talk to your customers about your product. That knowledge compounds, and nobody else can copy it.


### Synthetic users will love your idea. That's the problem.


AI-generated personas are tempting. They never cancel, they're available at 2 a.m., and they have thoughtful feedback on everything. They're also very, very nice.


When researchers at Nielsen Norman Group, the UX research firm founded by Jakob Nielsen and Don Norman, tested synthetic users, they found that[since AI loves to please, every idea is often seen as a good one](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/) . Unanimous applause feels great in a review, but it can be detrimental to choosing winning product bets.


Synthetic users shouldn't be the source of truth for a roadmap. Prioritization runs on knowing how strongly people feel and where they disagree, and that's where simulated feedback is weakest. Your real customers will tell you what to cut, and that's some of the most valuable feedback you'll ever get.


So give AI the jobs it's great at: drafting interview guides, summarizing transcripts, spotting patterns across dozens of conversations. Figma's research team describes the balance well. Peggy Zhang, AI Insights Program Manager on Figma's research team, says["AI doesn't replace research judgment, it raises the bar on it."](https://www.rallyuxr.com/case-study/figma) We think the same is true for product judgment.


### Customer discovery is only as good as who’s in the room


Every study rests on one thing: the people you talk to. If they’re the wrong people, the analysis, the readout and the roadmap decision built on top of it all inherit the problem.


For years, the default was to rent participants from a third-party panel. That’s getting harder to justify. Costs keep rising, and teams are finding more responses that look a little too polished, the kind written by a bot rather than a person. You end up paying more and second-guessing what you got back.


Your own customers don’t have that problem. They’ve used your product and have hit its rough edges. You can find them based on what they do in your product, not what they claim on a screener.


There’s a longer-term payoff too. A rented panel resets every time you run a study. A panel made of your own customers gets more useful the more you use it, because every conversation tells you a bit more about who to talk to next, who’s been contacted recently and who’s always happy to help. Over a year, that adds up to something no competitor can recreate.


The catch is that a customer panel needs to be run well. People need to opt in, nobody should get asked five times a month and the data needs to be handled carefully. That’s the part Rally takes care of. Our[CRM & Panel Management](https://rallyuxr.com/features/crm-and-panel-management) turns your customer base into a research panel your whole team can use responsibly, so every study starts with the right people.


### Builders learn the most when they hear it firsthand


Rally's vision is simple: Every product team talks to their users. We mean the PMs, designers and engineers who decide what gets built, talking to customers every week. Research reports are useful, but a PM who has actually watched a customer struggle with a workflow can make a sharper, more empathetic call.


That includes engineers. When an engineer watches a customer get stuck on a workflow, the fix often shows up in the next sprint without anyone needing to write a ticket about it.


Rally customers show what this looks like in practice:


- **MongoDB:** More than 70 people across the company now run research, and PMs, engineers and product leadership can watch customer sessions live. Product Design Lead Ksenia Samokhvalova says["It brings the user voice directly into product conversations."](https://www.rallyuxr.com/case-study/mongodb)
- **Earnest:** Principal UX Researcher Ellie Moskova says the team can now do[research closer to the beginning of the product cycle](https://www.rallyuxr.com/case-study/earnest) , when it can still shape the plan.
- **Included Health:** The team ran[about four times as much research](https://www.rallyuxr.com/case-study/included-health) in a year while keeping costs down.


In each case, researchers set the standard for quality and product teams get close to customers. Everybody wins, especially your users.


### Teams that talk to users make their leaders look great


When your product and design teams talk to customers every week, you get better as a leader too.


**Walk into roadmap reviews with receipts.** When the CEO or board asks why a bet made the cut, you answer with what customers said and showed you. Leadership sees your roadmap as a set of informed bets, and that track record earns you more trust, more budget and more room to make the next call your way.


**Make** **braver bets.** Evidence gives you the confidence to back an ambitious idea, and the cover to pass on a weak one without hurting anyone's feelings.


**Get** **more out of the team you have.** Engineering time is your most expensive resource. When customer conversations reshape a bet in its first week, the sprints you would have spent on the wrong thing go to work that moves your metrics. That's more impact from the same headcount.


**Your team is happier.** People want to know their work matters, and customers are the most convincing people to tell them.


**Your people grow faster.** Strong PMs and designers want to understand users deeply. Giving them direct access is one of the best development opportunities you can offer as a leader.


**The whole company trusts Product more.** Sales, customer success and your CEO all have opinions about what Product should build. When your team can show what customers said, roadmap debates get shorter and the rest of the company gets behind your plan.


### Habits of product orgs that learn fast


We work with product teams at companies like Figma, Ramp, Meta, Perplexity, and more, and the ones making the best calls have made customer conversations a normal part of the week. Across Rally customers, those teams share the same five habits:


**Every big bet has customers behind it.** Any initiative bigger than a few weeks of work gets a handful of real conversations before it gets staffed.


**The builders are in the room.** PMs and designers lead conversations, and engineers listen in or join the conversations regularly.


**Learning runs on a weekly rhythm.** A few conversations every week beat one big study a quarter.


**Researchers set the bar.** Research teams define what good looks like and coach everyone else, so quality rises as volume grows.


**AI handles the busywork.** Scheduling, summaries and logistics get automated, so time can be spent on the conversation and the decision.


### Three Claude prompts for product leaders


These work with resources you already have, and each one takes about five minutes.


### 1.


Pressure-test your roadmap before planning


Paste in your roadmap or planning doc, plus any customer notes you have. You get a table showing which bets are backed by customer evidence and which are running on opinion, plus the fastest way to close each gap. Use it a week or two before quarterly planning.


```text
You are helping a VP of Product prepare for quarterly planning. Below is our roadmap and any customer evidence we have. For each initiative, create a table with: the initiative, the customer problem it assumes, the evidence we have (quote it, or write "none"), an evidence rating (strong, some, none), and the single riskiest assumption. Then list the three bets most worth validating with customers in the next two weeks, and for each one, the five customers or segments we should talk to and the one question that would change our mind.


Roadmap: [paste or point Claude to where it's located]
Customer evidence: [paste notes, transcripts, research, or leave blank]
```


### 2.


Find the patterns across everything customers tell you


Paste in support tickets, sales notes, NPS comments or interview notes. You get the top themes with how often they come up, who's raising them and the best customer quotes, mapped against your current bets. Use it monthly to spot what your roadmap is missing.


```text
Below is customer feedback from several sources. Group it into the top 5 to 8 themes. For each theme, give: a one-line summary, roughly how many pieces of feedback mention it, which customer segments raise it most, and two direct quotes. Then compare the themes to our current roadmap: which themes our bets address, which they ignore, and any feedback that contradicts a bet we've already committed to. Keep it to one page.


Feedback: [paste or point Claude to where it's located]
Current roadmap bets: [paste or point Claude to where it's located]
```


### 3.


Turn customer conversations into an exec-ready update


Paste in notes or transcripts from your team's conversations on a bet. You get a one-page readout for your CEO or leadership team: what you learned, what you're changing and why, with customer quotes as proof. Use it before roadmap reviews.


```text
I'm a VP of Product updating my CEO and leadership team. Below are notes from our customer conversations about [initiative]. Write a one-page update with these sections: what we set out to learn, what customers told us (with 3 short direct quotes), what surprised us, our decision (continue, change, or stop) and why, and what we need from leadership. Write it for busy executives: plain language, no jargon, under 300 words.


Conversation notes: [paste or point Claude to where it's located]
```


### You'll know it's working when


- More roadmap bets have customer conversations behind them
- The time from a product question to the first customer conversation is measured in days
- More PMs, designers and engineers talked to a customer this month than last
- Your team shares customer clips in planning meetings without being asked


### Start with one conversation this week


AI handed your team the ability to build almost anything. The edge in 2027 belongs to the teams that know what's worth building, and that starts with talking to your own users every week. We're building toward a world where every product team talks to their users, and we'd love for yours to be next.
